newsitem.title: RUSSIA: New joint Mir crew to get down to repair business.
newsitem.headline: New joint Mir crew to get down to repair business.

text.p: The three tired men and their two fresh replacements now aboard the crippled Mir space station face a busy seven-day handover period starting on Friday after a difficult but successful docking on Thursday.

Flight Director Vladimir Solovyov told reporters at Mission Control outside Moscow the cosmonauts would first have to deal with oxygen supplies. The current crew earlier on Thursday failed to fix the Elektron system and said more time was needed.
They now burn oxygen "candles", the only oxygen source on Mir when it started orbiting the Earth 11 years ago. Officials say they have enough reserves but the system has to be fixed.

Solovyov also said current commander Vasily Tsibliyev, 43, who had developed heart problems, and flight engineer Alexander Lazutkin have to undergo thorough medical tests and physical training ahead of their return to Earth on August 14.

They will also have to show the incoming commander, space veteran Anatoly Solovyov, 49, and 43-year-old novice flight engineer Pavel Vinogradov what is stored where at the station, Flight Director Solovyov (eds: no relation) said.

A U.S. NASA agency astronaut, British-American physicist Michael Foale, will stay until late September when NASA astronaut David Wolf, who is now in training outside Moscow, is scheduled to replace him.
After the departure of the current crew, the remaining team will face an even more difficult task of restoring power to Mir and sealing a hole in the punctured Spektr scientific module.
Mir suffered its worst accident on June 25, when a supply ship pierced Spektr during a manual docking manoeuvre.
Cosmonauts had to unplug power cables leading from Spektr's solar panels as they fled the module and sealed it. The accident deprived Mir of up to half of its power supply.

Space officials decided to delay repairing the Spektr after Tsibliyev developed heart trouble and then the crew plunged into another crisis by accidentally unplugging a vital computer, causing the station to lose its orientation for more than a day.
Solovyov and Vinogradov will don space suits on August 20 and enter the airless, darkened Spektr to reconnect the cables.
"The crew which has arrived at Mir is perfectly trained and I think they'll be able to fulfil all the tasks," said Yuri Koptev, head of Russia's Space Agency.

The next major task for the new crew would be to locate and fix the puncture in the Spektr and Koptev said up to six space walks had been scheduled for the operation. But he added that the crew might well be able to cope in two or three sorties.
On September 3, Foale is due to take part in a space walk with commander Solovyov to find the hole in the Spektr.
The docking of Mir and Soyuz spacecraft on Thursday was not an easy one and the relief crew had to dock manually when automatic systems developed a fault 13 metres (yards) from Mir.
"Soyuz retreated by 25 metres and then docked manually," Flight Director Solovyov told reporters. "It was a technical malfunction. The situation was not a critical one but we will look into it."

Despite the hitch, Russia's top space official seemed happy and applause burst out at the tense Mission Control outside Moscow and a huge sign "Congratulations" appeared on the screen after the docking at 1702 GMT, a minute ahead of schedule.
At 1830 GMT, as scheduled, the hatches between Mir and Soyuz opened and live television pictures showed the cosmonauts smiling and hugging.
They floated in Mir's weightlessness, worked on cables and secured bolts as they made final touches to the link-up.
A spokesman for the Mission Control outside Moscow said the cosmonauts would have dinner after the work was finished.

"They will have dinner but we should not call it a festive one," said Vsevolod Latyshev. "They may have a special drink based on alcohol which has been prepared by the Institute of Medical and Biological Problems."
